title: Elements, Tags, and Attributes
description: Master the difference between tags and elements, and give your buttons modifiers using attributes.

primaryCapability.statement: Distinguish between tags and elements, and apply boolean attributes inside opening tags.

objectives.description: Identify the anatomy of an HTML element and place an attribute correctly inside the opening tag.

content.title: Nouns, Adjectives, and the Whole Sandwich
content.hook: Junior devs mix up 'tag' and 'element' all the time. Let's fix that forever in 30 seconds.
content.context: A tag is just the bracketed label like <button>. The entire sandwich—from <button> all the way to </button>—is the Element. Now, what if you want to modify that button? You slip an Attribute inside the opening tag, like an adjective.
goals: Understand the difference between a Tag and an Element
Add the 'disabled' attribute to shut off button clicks

content.question: Which button element has an attribute attached that tells the browser: 'Freeze this, don't let anyone click it'?

options.previewHtml: <button style='padding: 10px 22px; background: #ea580c; color: white; border: none; border-radius: 10px; font-weight: 700; cursor: pointer;'>Submit</button>
<button disabled style='padding: 10px 22px; background: #52525b; color: #a1a1aa; border: none; border-radius: 10px; font-weight: 700; cursor: not-allowed; opacity: 0.6;'>Submit</button>

content.explanation: The word 'disabled' placed inside the opening tag is an attribute. It modifies the element's default behavior.

feedback.correct: Bullseye! 'disabled' is a boolean attribute. Simply writing it inside the opening tag turns the button off.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the button with the extra word tucked inside the opening bracket: <button disabled>.

content.prompt: Disable this button so users can't click it twice:

blanks.hint: What standard attribute freezes a button?

content.explanation: HTML keywords are specific. Browsers recognize 'disabled', not custom words like 'off' or 'stop'.

feedback.correct: Clean code! Notice how the attribute lives inside the opening <button> tag, separated by a single space.
feedback.incorrect: Browsers are literal robots. Tap 'disabled' from the Word Bank.

content.prompt: Inspect this snippet. What will the browser actually do when this renders?
options: Hide the button completely from the page
Show a warning popup when tapped
content.explanation: The 'disabled' attribute doesn't hide elements or show alerts; it visually mutes them and strips user interaction.

feedback.correct: Precisely. The element stays visible on screen, but the browser blocks all clicks and dims its appearance.
feedback.incorrect: Attributes alter behavior, not existence. The button will still be drawn, but you won't be able to click it.

content.prompt: Assemble a complete disabled button element in the right order:
content.explanation: Attributes ONLY go into the opening tag. The closing tag is always just </button>.

feedback.correct: Flawless. Opening tag with attribute -> label -> clean closing tag.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: Opening tag on the left (<button disabled>), text in the middle, closing tag on the right (</button>).

content.question: A junior dev wrote </button disabled> to close a tag. What's the verdict?

options.text: Wrong! Attributes NEVER go in closing tags.
Correct! You must repeat attributes in both tags.
It works, but it's considered bad practice.

content.explanation: Closing tags exist solely to mark where an element ends. Putting attributes inside </button> is invalid HTML—the browser treats closing tags as strictly </tagname>.

feedback.correct: You saved the codebase! Attributes belong strictly in the opening tag. Putting them on the closing tag is like putting mayo on the outside of your sandwich wrapper.
feedback.incorrect: Closing tags never accept attributes. All modifiers must be declared in the opening tag.

content.title: Level 2 Cleared
takeaways: Tag vs Element: The tag is just <button>. The Element is the entire sandwich from <button> to </button>.
Attributes: Modifiers that live inside the opening tag (e.g., <button disabled>).
The Golden Rule: Closing tags NEVER take attributes. They just shut the door.
nextSteps: Next in 1.1.3: Headings & Paragraphs — moving past buttons to build real typographic layout.
